title: Acute otitis media: Streptococcus pneumoniae
vignette: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the clinic due to left ear pain over the past 3 days. Last week, the patient developed a runny nose and cough, which resolved 2 days prior to the development of ear pain. He has no chronic medical conditions. Temperature is 38.4 C (101.1 F). There is purulent drainage from the left ear. Otoscopic examination of the left ear reveals a normal-appearing external canal and an erythematous tympanic membrane with purulent fluid pooling within the distal external canal. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of this patient's diagnosis?

clues.text: Last week, the patient developed a runny nose and cough
clues.note: A preceding viral upper respiratory infection causes eustachian tube edema/obstruction, setting up acute otitis media.
An inflamed (erythematous, often bulging) tympanic membrane is the diagnostic sign of acute otitis media - a MIDDLE ear infection.

clues.text: purulent fluid pooling within the distal external canal
clues.note: Purulent drainage into the ear canal here reflects a perforated tympanic membrane from middle-ear suppuration (otitis media), not a primary canal infection.

whatMatters: A young child with a preceding viral URI, fever, an erythematous (perforated) tympanic membrane, and purulent drainage = acute otitis media (a MIDDLE-ear infection). The most common bacterial cause is STREPTOCOCCUS PNEUMONIAE (then nontypeable H. influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis). Answer F.
strategy: Localize to the MIDDLE ear (inflamed TM after a URI) = acute otitis media, then recall its top pathogens: S. pneumoniae (#1) > nontypeable H. influenzae > M. catarrhalis. Don't be misled by canal drainage into choosing otitis externa organisms (Pseudomonas, S. aureus) - the drainage here is from a ruptured TM. Reject Klebsiella and Proteus (not typical AOM causes).

eliminations.label: Klebsiella pneumoniae - not a typical AOM cause
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a gram-negative rod causing pneumonia (often in alcohol use/aspiration) and UTIs. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is an uncommon cause of acute otitis media in a healthy child. ✅ Correct if: aspiration pneumonia with currant-jelly sputum.

eliminations.label: Moraxella catarrhalis - possible but less common (your pick)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a respiratory colonizer and the THIRD most common cause of AOM. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it does cause AOM, but S. pneumoniae is MORE common and is the best single answer. ✅ Correct if: the question asked for a less common typical AOM organism after pneumococcus/H. influenzae.

eliminations.label: Proteus mirabilis - urinary pathogen
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a urease-positive gram-negative rod causing UTIs/struvite stones. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is not a cause of acute otitis media. ✅ Correct if: alkaline urine with struvite kidney stones.

eliminations.label: Pseudomonas aeruginosa - otitis EXTERNA / swimmer's ear
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a gram-negative rod causing otitis externa (swimmer's ear) and malignant otitis externa in diabetics. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: this is otitis MEDIA (inflamed TM after a URI), and the external canal is normal - the drainage is from a perforated TM. ✅ Correct if: painful swollen ear canal after water exposure (otitis externa).

eliminations.label: Staphylococcus aureus - skin/soft tissue, otitis externa
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a gram-positive coccus colonizing skin, implicated in otitis externa and skin infections. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is a colonizer of skin rather than the respiratory tract and is not a leading AOM cause. ✅ Correct if: otitis externa/skin and soft tissue infection.

reasoning: Young child + preceding viral URI + fever + erythematous (perforated) TM with purulent drainage = acute otitis media (middle ear)
AOM follows eustachian tube obstruction and overgrowth of respiratory colonizers
Most common bacterial cause is Streptococcus pneumoniae (then nontypeable H. influenzae, Moraxella)
mechanism: Acute otitis media (AOM) most often follows a viral upper respiratory infection: mucosal inflammation obstructs the eustachian tube, so middle-ear secretions cannot drain and accumulate, providing a rich medium for bacterial overgrowth. The bacteria are respiratory-tract colonizers of the nasopharynx that proliferate in the trapped secretions; the most common is STREPTOCOCCUS PNEUMONIAE, followed by nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis. Suppuration raises middle-ear pressure and inflames/bulges the tympanic membrane; if pressure is high enough the TM can rupture, releasing purulent fluid into the external canal (as here, with an otherwise normal-appearing canal). AOM is most common in young children (age 6 months to 2 years) because of their short, horizontal eustachian tubes. The Pseudomonas/S. aureus options are causes of otitis EXTERNA (canal infection), which this is not.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Micro/ENT > acute otitis media: preceded by viral URI, eustachian tube obstruction; top causes S. pneumoniae > nontypeable H. influenzae > M. catarrhalis; otitis externa = Pseudomonas/S. aureus.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Inflamed TM after a URI = otitis MEDIA; its #1 cause is S. pneumoniae (canal drainage is from TM rupture, not otitis externa).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on otitis media vs externa, tympanic membrane perforation, eustachian tube, or nontypeable H. influenzae? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Pseudomonas/S. aureus = otitis externa; Moraxella is a real but less common AOM cause; Klebsiella/Proteus aren't AOM organisms.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: acute otitis media top 3 = S. pneumoniae, nontypeable H. influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis; follows viral URI.
